content:
Apple has long made privacy a selling point of both its hardware and its services, but I sometimes wonder whether it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

A seemingly narrowly-scoped measure which every few months faces a new antitrust lawsuit or investigation by a regulator. There's now a third UK case involving ATT — and this one is a little different.

Apple's response is added to the end of the article …

The personalized ads debate

Personalized advertising has long been a hot topic in the tech world. Why show us random ads we may have no interest in at all, when you can show us ads based on our interests — gathered from the apps we use and the websites we visit?

In theory, it benefits everyone. Consumers see ads they might actually be interested in; advertisers get a better return on their spend because they can target audiences more precisely; and free apps and websites which rely on ad revenue earn more for the same reason.

Even where the data used to serve personalized ads is collected anonymously, it's widely regarded by the general public as an invasion of privacy. Despite Apple specifically developing a technology to ensure that data is anonymous, many consumers remain skeptical.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's ATT was intended to solve this by giving consumers a choice. Developers wanting to collect this kind of data must first get consumer consent.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, the measure has attracted a string of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, primarily because Apple's own apps don't have to ask for the same consent. Apple has repeatedly stressed that its rules apply equally: its own apps don't show the ATT prompt because they don't collect this kind of data in the first place. Third-party apps that don't collect this data are also exempt from the prompt.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three complaints filed with the UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal (the relevant antitrust regulator). It lost the first case, and is now appealing; the second case is still ongoing.

The third lawsuit was reported by Reuters, and has today been formally filed.

What's new

There's an interesting twist to the latest lawsuit: the claimant is Ann Pope, a former senior official at the relevant regulator.

Pope, who is leading the case, formerly served as a senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority. She said Apple's policies have "caused very significant harm to businesses that rely on Apple as a gatekeeper." Pope said in a statement: "This case is critical to protecting the rights of UK businesses that rely on Apple, ensuring the rules Apple adopts are fair, and securing compensation for UK companies for the losses they have suffered."

Following an investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator, Apple recently agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules to comply with EU demands. Regarding this lawsuit, Apple gave us the following response:

Over the years, many privacy advocates have publicly expressed their support for ATT.
